title: Knowledge Check 1: Lessons 1-8
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 1-8 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Which split correctly describes the two architect domains?
options: System: integration and identity; Application: data and sharing
System: data and sharing; Application: integration and identity
System: end-user training; Application: release governance
System: native features; Application: security reviews
questions.explanation: The Application Architect owns everything inside the org, such as the data model and sharing, while the System Architect owns what crosses between systems: integration, identity, and release governance.

questions.question: Why is the boundary between the two architect roles drawn where it is?
options: Because one role applies only to small orgs and the other only to enterprise orgs.
Because the two roles are graded by two different vendor exams.
Because one role stays inside the org and the other crosses trust boundaries.
Because one role is declarative work and the other is entirely code.
questions.explanation: The Application Architect's concerns stay inside a single trust boundary (the org), while the System Architect's concerns cross trust boundaries between systems.

questions.question: What does the pinnacle architect credential require beyond the domain certifications?
options: Three separate multiple-choice exams covering every certification domain
Documented real work and a scenario defense before a review board
A recertification pass every six months.
A written recommendation from three prior employers.
questions.explanation: The pinnacle credential requires both domain credentials plus documented real work and a live review-board defense, so it cannot be earned by study alone.

questions.question: What does it mean that Salesforce is a multi-tenant platform?
options: Many tenants share one platform, with each org's data isolated.
Each customer gets a dedicated database server and its own schema.
Customers own the hardware their org runs on but share the license.
All tenants share one schema with no separation between records.
questions.explanation: Multi-tenancy means the platform runs many orgs on shared infrastructure, but each org's data is isolated by its OrgID.

questions.question: What is the guiding rule for arranging an environment ladder?
options: Every environment should hold a full copy of production data.
The production org doubles as the release rehearsal environment.
Each environment answers a question the one below it cannot.
Developer sandboxes are reserved for user acceptance testing.
questions.explanation: The ladder exists so each test question is answered by the cheapest environment capable of answering it, with a full copy reserved for release rehearsal.

questions.question: Why do governor limits push developers toward bulk, collection-based processing?
options: Because synchronous REST calls are always slower than asynchronous bulk calls.
Because limits cap per-transaction work to protect shared resources.
Because bulk processing always produces more accurate data.
Because small orgs are exempt from the platform's resource limits.
questions.explanation: Limits exist to keep one tenant from monopolizing shared resources, so code must process records in bulk within a single transaction budget.

questions.question: What does a master-detail relationship provide that a lookup relationship does not?
options: Inherited detail security and roll-up summaries on the master.
An independent security model and a visible Owner field on the detail.
A way to relate two objects that otherwise have no relationship.
The ability to store one record inside two different objects.
questions.explanation: Master-detail makes the master own the detail, so the detail inherits the master's security and ownership and roll-ups become available; a lookup supports neither.

questions.question: When should an architect choose a roll-up summary instead of a formula field?
options: When a value can be computed from fields within a single record.
When the value must update in real time on each record view.
When a value aggregates many child records onto the master.
When the value must be shown on a report or a list view.
questions.explanation: Roll-up summaries aggregate COUNT, SUM, MIN, or MAX from related child records onto a master, which a formula cannot do.

questions.question: What are record types intended to model?
options: Genuinely different fields and visibility between two business units.
Different processes, picklists, and layouts within one data shape.
Separate objects that share a single field set and sharing model.
A way to control which existing records a user is allowed to view.
questions.explanation: Record types vary the process, picklist values, and layout for one object; they share one field set and sharing model and do not gate record visibility.

questions.question: When sizing an integration, which decision should come first?
options: Whether the caller can wait for a response.
Which API the architect prefers to use.
Which format the source system already speaks.
How many licenses the org happens to own.
questions.explanation: Whether the caller can wait separates synchronous from asynchronous options before volume and format matter.

questions.question: Which condition makes Bulk API 2.0 the right choice over a synchronous API?
options: A single record that must be confirmed before the user continues.
A call that needs a strongly typed, compile-time WSDL contract to catch errors.
A large volume where the caller does not need to wait for the result.
A small batch that must all succeed or fail as one operation.
questions.explanation: Bulk is asynchronous and built for scale, so it fits large volumes where no one is waiting, while small or all-or-nothing calls stay synchronous.

questions.question: What does the REST Composite resource let an architect do?
options: Run a large query asynchronously and collect its results hours later.
Fold up to 25 subrequests into one call that counts once.
Bypass the per-org request limits for very high-volume operations.
Encrypt payloads end to end between two connected systems.
questions.explanation: Composite folds several subrequests into one HTTP call that counts as a single request, which keeps a modest batch from consuming many calls.

questions.question: Which three things does a system's architecture fundamentally comprise?
options: Its components, their relationships, and its principles.
Its vendors, its operating budget, and its release schedule.
Its users, their permissions, and their reporting needs.
Its servers, its network links, and its software licenses.
questions.explanation: Architecture is defined by a system's components, how those components relate, and the principles that keep the design coherent as it changes.

questions.question: Why is naming a design pattern not the same as having an architecture?
options: A pattern always names the specific technology and vendor a system is built on.
A pattern guarantees the system will scale without any further work.
A pattern is a starting point; architecture adds the resilience around it.
A pattern is only valid for software written in one programming language.
questions.explanation: A pattern describes a coordination shape; architecture is what makes that shape survive production through error handling, state persistence, security, and retry.

questions.question: What do coordination patterns such as pipes, map-reduce, and circuit breakers have in common across software and AI systems?
options: Each pattern requires its own specialized hardware to run.
The patterns stay stable while the processing units change.
They only apply to systems that process text and language.
They were all invented specifically for modern AI agent systems.
questions.explanation: The same coordination shapes recur for decades and reappear in AI systems, because only the processing units change, not the underlying patterns.

questions.question: When should an integration use the request-reply pattern?
options: When the caller must wait and act on the response immediately.
When the caller hands off the work and never waits for any result.
When large volumes move on a nightly schedule.
When data must be replicated in bulk in either direction.
questions.explanation: Request-reply is synchronous: the caller blocks for the response and updates its state from it, which only works for small, real-time interactions.

questions.question: Why does a fire-and-forget integration usually need a callback?
options: Because the event bus guarantees delivery to every subscriber.
Because platform events can be rolled back just like ordinary database transactions.
Because the remote system processes later and its key is not known yet.
Because the caller must block until the remote process has finished.
questions.explanation: Because the handoff is asynchronous, the remote system reports its created key back through a callback rather than returning it in the original call.

questions.question: What makes a batch data synchronization a good fit?
options: A single record that must be confirmed while a user waits.
A large volume where timeliness matters less than throughput and safety.
A payment that must be authorized and displayed before the page returns.
A change that must reach a warehouse within one second.
questions.explanation: Batch moves large volumes on a schedule, so it is chosen when throughput and safe, re-runnable loads matter more than immediate updates.

questions.question: What distinguishes a Platform Event from Change Data Capture?
options: A Platform Event carries a designed payload for business intent; CDC carries record state.
A Platform Event only ever reports record deletions, while CDC reports only record creations.
A Platform Event needs no subscriber, while CDC requires a custom payload.
A Platform Event lives only in memory, while CDC is written to disk.
questions.explanation: Platform Events let you define a message for business intent, while CDC automatically publishes the changed record's fields, noise from bulk loads included.

questions.question: How should a consumer reconstruct the order of CDC changes from one save?
options: Sort every event by its ReplayId, which is contiguous and unique.
Trust commitNumber, which is a guaranteed and globally unique key for ordering events.
Assume the event bus delivers every change in strict global order.
Group by transactionKey, then order within the group by sequenceNumber.
questions.explanation: The bus does not guarantee strict order, so consumers group by transactionKey and use sequenceNumber within a transaction, treating commitNumber as diagnostic.

questions.question: Why must a subscriber persist and reuse its ReplayId?
options: To convert a Platform Event stream into a Change Data Capture stream.
To resume a stream after a disconnect and catch up on missed events.
To raise the daily delivery allocation available to the org.
To make replay IDs contiguous and simple to compute by hand.
questions.explanation: Replay IDs mark a position in the stream, so storing the last one lets a consumer reconnect and replay missed events within the retention window.

questions.question: Why does a middleware hub beat point-to-point wiring as systems multiply?
options: Pairwise connections grow with the square of the system count; a hub grows linearly.
Point-to-point wiring is always faster to build and far cheaper to maintain over time.
A hub removes the need for any authentication between connected systems.
Point-to-point connections stop working once three systems exist.
questions.explanation: Every pair of systems needs its own connection, so point-to-point count grows with the square of systems while a hub needs each system to connect only once.

questions.question: Under the orchestration test, when does an integration genuinely need middleware?
options: When it makes one synchronous call to a single system and returns a value.
When it only needs to schedule a nightly bulk transfer between two systems.
When it needs complex flow logic, aggregation, transformation, or transactional integrity.
When it must display live external data inside the org without ever copying it into local storage.
questions.explanation: Middleware earns its cost only for real orchestration: complex flow logic, aggregation across systems, transformation, or transactional integrity that spans systems.

questions.question: Why is the true cost of a custom integration higher than its build cost suggests?
options: Custom code always requires a recurring per-user software license.
Most of the total cost is maintenance spread over years.
Custom integrations cannot be monitored or tested in any way.
The build cost is fixed while maintenance turns out to be free.
questions.explanation: Development is only a fraction of a custom integration's cost, because updates, API changes, retesting, and adaptations consume most of the total over its life.
